title: Bishops 1V1
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and complete native diagrams reviewed. Final mating pattern only, beginning after Be5 at139 seconds. Native39 shows the king on c4 with Black’s bishop still on d4; native40 confirms Be5 and native41 confirms Bd3 mate. The complete twelve-piece diagram has White Kc4/Be2/b7/d2/g2 against Ke4/Be5/a7/c6/f7/f4/h4. White can play Bd3# immediately. A finite certificate establishes this exact later win by actual mate, without discarding any pawn or using an engine estimate. This does not prove that Be5 was forced or certify the earlier d4/Bf3/Be2 displacement, bishop-capture alternative, premature promotion comparison or the original fourteen-piece setup. Those larger outcomes remain separate analysis requirements.
transcript: White is trying to promote to a new queen, but there is an issue. Now, the black bishop can give a check, and after the king moves, it can come to D6 and prevent the promotion like this. And now, with all of this extra pawn, black is the only one playing for an advantage. So, white's only hope to get an advantage in this position is to make sure that this black bishop can never prevent the promotion. But luckily, white has an incredible resource in this position. Of course, we start with D4 check, trying to misplace this king. If the king goes, for example, to F5, now after we take and the bishop gives this check and we come up, the bishop cannot come to D6 to stop the promotion. The king would simply take it. So, the black king has to somehow defend the bishop that wants to stop the promotion. But if the king comes up to E6, now there's going to be bishop to G4 check, forcing the king to move again. Except that the king doesn't have to move. It can cover with F5. But remember, all we want to achieve is to dislodge this king. So, in this position, white has the pretty obvious sacrifice, bishop takes F4. And after the king takes, we can promote without any problem. The bishop can give us a check, but there's nothing to do. After this, we're going to take the bishop and win the game. So, black has to become a little bit creative here and try to go down to E4. And at first, this doesn't seem to make any sense. If we try to take here and promote now, this square is not defended. But unfortunately, black is preparing another idea with bishop takes D4 check like this. And now, the bishop can come to defend from here and we lose. So, white has to keep trying dislodging this king. For example, with bishop to F3 check. Of course, if the king goes back up, we can simply promote. So, the black king has to try D3, from where it can still defend this check of the bishop. But white is not done with her brilliant resources and plays the beautiful bishop E2, sacrificing the bishop completely. Because of course, if the bishop is taken, now we can promote and there is no way for this bishop to stop the promotion. But you would be foolish to think that this is the end of the story because naturally this black king is free to go back to e4 like this. And now we might have at the very least secured the draw with this shuffling of the bishop, but that is not what white wants. And here white decides to finally take the pawn. But this doesn't seem to make any sense. Can't black just give us this check and then come back to stop the promotion like this? And the answer is no. Because incredibly out of nowhere white has created a mating net. And bishop to d3 ends the game with a checkmate. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
